Gung-ho
GUNG-HOH
adjective (Silent Generation slang)
From Chinese gung ho (Mandarin gong he), "work together," a slogan of the Chinese Industrial Cooperatives of the late 1930s. Marine Lt. Col. Evans F. Carlson, who had observed Chinese forces in the 1930s, adopted it as the motto of his 2nd Marine Raider Battalion in 1942, and the 1943 film Gung Ho!, about the Raiders’ Makin Island raid, made it national. By the later 1940s it had come to mean eager, zealous, all in — and sometimes overzealous.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

When Grandpa’s generation said a man was gung-ho, they meant he was all in — first up in the morning, first to volunteer, the last to quit. The word came from the Marines, and the Marines got it from China: it was a slogan meaning "work together," which Colonel Evans Carlson gave his Raiders in 1942. Notice that: the original gung-ho was not one man’s fire but a whole unit pulling as one. Scripture likes that. "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour" (Ecc 4:9), and "a threefold cord is not quickly broken" (Ecc 4:12). When Nehemiah’s people rebuilt Jerusalem’s wall under threat, it rose fast, "for the people had a mind to work" (Neh 4:6). Paul wanted the church to stand "with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel" (Php 1:27). There is a warning too. Zeal without wisdom can run a man into trouble, and Paul grieved over people who had "a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge" (Rom 10:2). The perfect example of right zeal is Christ Himself, who cleansed His Father’s house so that His disciples remembered, "The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up" (Joh 2:17). He was all in for His Father’s glory, all the way to the cross, and He did it to make one people out of many. A Christian should be gung-ho in the first sense — eager, wholehearted, and pulling together.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (WWII Marine Corps, from a Chinese slogan meaning "work together") for zealous, wholehearted, all in — zeal Scripture commends when it pulls together and is according to knowledge (Rom 10:2).

expand to see more

GUNG-HO, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; Marine Corps, from Chinese "work together") Zealously enthusiastic; eager and wholehearted, sometimes to excess. "The new lieutenant is awful gung-ho."

Decode for families: gung-ho first meant "work together" — the best zeal is shared, and it knows what it is zealous for.

Key Scripture

Ecc 4:9 — "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour."

Neh 4:6 — "So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work."

Php 1:27 — "Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;"

Rom 10:2 — "For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge."

Joh 2:17 — "And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up."

Modern Corruption

An honourable word for wholehearted effort; the only caution is zeal without knowledge — the eager man who outruns wisdom or his comrades.

expand to see more

There is nothing wrong with being gung-ho. The word was born in a Marine battalion that trained hard and fought together, and its first meaning — work together — is a fine one for any family or church. Scripture praises a people with a mind to work (Neh 4:6).

The word later picked up an edge: the gung-ho man can be the one who charges ahead without thinking, or who makes everyone else’s life hard by his eagerness. Paul’s warning fits him — zeal not according to knowledge (Rom 10:2). The cure is not less zeal but zeal aimed rightly, and shared.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Chinese gong he (work together; 1930s cooperative slogan) → 1942 motto of Carlson’s 2nd Marine Raiders → 1943 film Gung Ho! → 1940s American slang (zealous, all in).

expand to see more

Chinese gong (work) + he (together, in harmony)

Late 1930s: slogan of the Chinese Industrial Cooperatives

1942: motto of Lt. Col. Evans Carlson’s 2nd Marine Raider Battalion

1943: the film Gung Ho! spreads the word

Later 1940s–: gung-ho — eager, zealous, sometimes overzealous

Usage

""Uncle Walt was so gung-ho about the church roof he had the shingles up before the deacons finished voting.""

"Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour (Ecc 4:9)."

"So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work (Neh 4:6)."
